question: Which federal law prohibits discrimination in the sale, rental, and financing of housing based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability?
choice_a: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)
choice_b: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA)
choice_c: The Federal Fair Housing Act (Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as amended)
choice_d: The Truth in Lending Act (TILA)
explanation: The Federal Fair Housing Act, enacted as Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 and later amended, is the core federal statute prohibiting housing discrimination based on the seven protected classes.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §§ 3601-3619 (Fair Housing Act)

question: The Federal Fair Housing Act as originally passed in 1968 protected against discrimination based on race, color, religion, and national origin. Which protected class was added by amendment in 1974?
choice_a: Disability
choice_b: Familial status
choice_c: Age
choice_d: Sex
explanation: Sex was added as a protected class in 1974 through the Housing and Community Development Act, expanding the original four classes named in the 1968 Act.
source_note: Housing and Community Development Act of 1974, amending 42 U.S.C. § 3604

question: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added which two protected classes to the Federal Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: Disability (handicap) and familial status
choice_b: Sex and national origin
choice_c: Age and marital status
choice_d: Religion and source of income
explanation: The 1988 amendments extended fair housing protections to persons with disabilities and families with children, bringing the total number of federally protected classes to seven.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604, as amended by the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988

question: Under the Federal Fair Housing Act, the protected class of "familial status" applies to which group?
choice_a: Unmarried couples living together
choice_b: Families with one or more children under 18, including pregnant women and persons in the process of securing legal custody of a child
choice_c: Single adults living alone
choice_d: Multigenerational households of any composition
explanation: Familial status protects households with children under 18, pregnant women, and those securing custody of a minor, from housing discrimination such as being denied a rental because they have children.

question: Under the Federal Fair Housing Act's so-called "Mrs. Murphy" exemption, an owner-occupied dwelling with no more than how many units may be exempt from certain fair housing provisions, provided no discriminatory advertising is used and no real estate professional is involved?
choice_a: Two units
choice_b: Six units
choice_c: Four units, with the owner occupying one of them
choice_d: Eight units
explanation: The owner-occupied exemption applies to buildings of no more than four units where the owner lives in one of the units, so long as discriminatory advertising is not used.

question: Under the Federal Fair Housing Act, a private individual owner may be exempt from certain provisions when selling or renting a single-family home without a real estate licensee, provided the transactions are limited to what frequency and no discriminatory advertising is used?
choice_a: No more than one such sale or rental per year
choice_b: No more than five such sales or rentals in any 12-month period
choice_c: No limit, as long as the owner personally occupies the home
choice_d: No more than three such sales or rentals in any 24-month period
explanation: The private-individual exemption limits an owner without a real estate professional to no more than three such sales or rentals within any 24-month period, and prohibits discriminatory advertising.

question: Which of the following entities may lawfully give preference to their own members when selling, renting, or occupying non-commercially operated dwellings under a specific Federal Fair Housing Act exemption?
choice_a: Religious organizations and private clubs
choice_b: Franchised real estate brokerages
choice_c: Publicly traded property management companies
choice_d: Federally chartered banks
explanation: The Act exempts religious organizations and bona fide private clubs from certain fair housing provisions when they limit occupancy of non-commercial dwellings to their own members, as long as membership is not restricted based on a protected class the exemption doesn't cover.

question: Under the Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA), a "55 and older" community may lawfully exclude families with children if at least what percentage of its occupied units has at least one resident age 55 or older?
choice_a: 50 percent
choice_b: 80 percent
choice_c: 100 percent
choice_d: 62 percent
explanation: HOPA requires that at least 80% of occupied units have at least one occupant age 55 or older, along with published policies and procedures demonstrating intent to operate as 55-and-older housing, to qualify for the familial status exemption.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b)(2)(C) (Housing for Older Persons Act)

question: Although "sexual orientation" and "gender identity" are not explicitly listed as protected classes in the text of the Federal Fair Housing Act, HUD has taken the position that discrimination on these bases is unlawful because it constitutes what?
choice_a: A separate, explicitly enumerated protected class added by a 2020 amendment to the Act
choice_b: Discrimination based on national origin
choice_c: Discrimination "because of sex" under Section 3604, consistent with the U.S. Supreme Court's reasoning in Bostock v. Clayton County
choice_d: A state-law-only protection with no federal basis
explanation: Following the Supreme Court's 2020 Bostock decision interpreting "sex" discrimination under Title VII to include sexual orientation and gender identity, HUD issued guidance applying the same reasoning to the Fair Housing Act's sex discrimination prohibition.
source_note: HUD Memorandum (Feb. 11, 2021), applying Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644 (2020) to 42 U.S.C. § 3604

question: HUD's Equal Access Rule requires that HUD-assisted and HUD-insured housing programs be made available without regard to which factors?
choice_a: Political affiliation and immigration status
choice_b: Credit score and employment history
choice_c: Source of income only
choice_d: Sexual orientation, gender identity, and marital status
explanation: The Equal Access Rule ensures that core HUD housing programs are open to all eligible individuals regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity, or marital status.
source_note: 24 C.F.R. Part 5, HUD Equal Access Rule (2012, amended 2016 and 2021)

question: A lender or insurer that refuses to make loans or issue policies in specific neighborhoods based on the racial or ethnic composition of the residents, rather than on the creditworthiness of individual applicants, is engaging in what illegal practice?
choice_a: Redlining
choice_b: Blockbusting
choice_c: Steering
choice_d: Puffing
explanation: Redlining is the discriminatory denial of mortgage loans, insurance, or other services based on the demographic makeup of a neighborhood, rather than an assessment of individual applicants.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3605 (discrimination in residential real estate-related transactions)

question: A licensee who persuades homeowners to sell quickly, often at a below-market price, by suggesting that members of a particular protected class are moving into the neighborhood and will cause property values to decline, is engaging in what illegal practice?
choice_a: Redlining
choice_b: Blockbusting (panic peddling)
choice_c: Steering
choice_d: Disparate impact
explanation: Blockbusting, sometimes called panic peddling, involves inducing owners to sell by exploiting fears about the entry of protected-class individuals into a neighborhood, and is expressly prohibited under the Act.

question: Directing homebuyers or renters toward or away from particular neighborhoods based on their race, national origin, or other protected characteristic, rather than their stated preferences and needs, is known as what?
choice_a: Redlining
choice_b: Blockbusting
choice_c: Steering
choice_d: Disparate treatment only in lending
explanation: Steering occurs when a licensee limits or influences a client's housing choices based on a protected characteristic instead of the client's own criteria, violating the Fair Housing Act.

question: A fair housing claim alleging that a facially neutral policy, applied equally to everyone, nonetheless disproportionately harms members of a protected class regardless of the housing provider's intent, is based on what legal theory?
choice_a: Disparate treatment
choice_b: Constructive eviction
choice_c: Reasonable accommodation denial
choice_d: Disparate impact
explanation: Disparate impact liability does not require proof of discriminatory intent; it focuses on whether a neutral policy or practice produces a discriminatory effect on a protected class, as recognized by the Supreme Court.
source_note: Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

question: Intentionally treating a homebuyer or renter less favorably because of their membership in a protected class, such as quoting a higher rent to a family with children than to a similarly qualified applicant without children, is an example of what?
choice_a: Disparate treatment
choice_b: Disparate impact
choice_c: Redlining
choice_d: A legitimate business practice
explanation: Disparate treatment involves intentional, differential treatment of an individual because of a protected characteristic, which is directly prohibited under Section 3604 of the Fair Housing Act.

question: To help demonstrate compliance with fair housing advertising rules, real estate advertisements typically should include what?
choice_a: A disclaimer limiting liability for misprints
choice_b: The Equal Housing Opportunity logo, statement, or slogan
choice_c: The seller's personal contact information only
choice_d: A statement that financing is not available
explanation: HUD's Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines encourage use of the Equal Housing Opportunity logo, statement, or slogan in real estate advertising as an indicator of nondiscriminatory intent.
source_note: 24 C.F.R. Part 109, HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines

question: Which of the following advertising phrases would most likely violate the Federal Fair Housing Act's prohibition on discriminatory advertising?
choice_a: "Close to shopping"
choice_b: "Move-in ready"
choice_c: "No children"
choice_d: "Cozy starter home"
explanation: The Act prohibits advertisements that indicate a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class; "no children" expresses an unlawful preference based on familial status.

question: Which title of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires real estate offices, as places of public accommodation, to be accessible to individuals with disabilities?
choice_a: Title I
choice_b: Title V
choice_c: Title VII
choice_d: Title III
explanation: Title III of the ADA covers places of public accommodation, including real estate offices, requiring reasonable accessibility for individuals with disabilities.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §§ 12181-12189 (ADA Title III)

question: How do a "reasonable accommodation" and a "reasonable modification" differ under federal fair housing and disability law?
choice_a: A reasonable accommodation is a change to a rule or policy, generally at the housing provider's expense, while a reasonable modification is a structural change, typically paid for by the person requesting it
choice_b: They are legally identical terms with no practical distinction
choice_c: A reasonable accommodation applies only to rental housing, while a reasonable modification applies only to owned housing
choice_d: A reasonable modification must always be paid for by the housing provider, while an accommodation is paid for by the tenant
explanation: HUD and DOJ guidance distinguishes accommodations (policy or rule changes, usually provider-funded) from modifications (physical/structural changes, usually requester-funded, though public housing has different funding rules).
source_note: Joint Statement of HUD and DOJ on Reasonable Accommodations Under the Fair Housing Act (2004) and Reasonable Modifications (2008)

question: A housing provider with a strict "no pets" policy generally must make what exception for a tenant with a disability as a reasonable accommodation?
choice_a: Waiving all rent payments
choice_b: Allowing the tenant to keep a service or assistance/emotional support animal
choice_c: Providing free veterinary care
choice_d: Relocating the tenant to a different building
explanation: Assistance animals are not considered pets under fair housing law, and a no-pets policy generally must be waived as a reasonable accommodation for a tenant who needs an assistance animal because of a disability.
source_note: Joint Statement of HUD and DOJ on Reasonable Accommodations Under the Fair Housing Act (2004)

question: The IRS "common law" test for distinguishing an employee from an independent contractor focuses primarily on what factor?
choice_a: Whether the worker holds a real estate license
choice_b: The worker's age and years of experience
choice_c: The degree of behavioral and financial control the employer/broker exercises over how the work is performed
choice_d: Whether the worker is paid by commission or salary
explanation: The IRS common law test looks at behavioral control, financial control, and the type of relationship between the parties to determine whether sufficient control exists to establish an employer-employee relationship.
source_note: IRS common law employee classification test

question: Under Internal Revenue Code Section 3508, a licensed real estate agent qualifies as a "statutory nonemployee" (independent contractor) for federal tax purposes if which three conditions are met?
choice_a: The individual works fewer than 20 hours per week and has no assigned desk
choice_b: The individual is over age 21 and has at least two years of industry experience
choice_c: The individual is paid a fixed salary regardless of sales performance
choice_d: The individual is a licensed real estate agent, substantially all compensation is directly tied to sales or output rather than hours worked, and services are performed under a written contract stating the agent will not be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes
explanation: IRC Section 3508 sets out a specific three-part statutory test that, if satisfied, treats a licensed real estate agent as a nonemployee for federal employment tax purposes, regardless of common law control factors.

question: Two competing brokerages agreeing to charge an identical, fixed commission rate to all of their clients would most likely violate which federal law?
choice_a: The Sherman Antitrust Act
choice_b: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
choice_c: The Fair Housing Act
choice_d: The Telephone Consumer Protection Act
explanation: Agreements between competitors to fix prices, including commission rates, are a per se violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, regardless of whether the fixed price is considered reasonable.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1-2

question: When several brokers conspire to exclude a competing broker from an MLS or agree to refuse to do business with a particular firm in order to eliminate competition, this antitrust violation is called what?
choice_a: Market allocation
choice_b: Group boycotting
choice_c: Tying arrangement
choice_d: Price fixing
explanation: A group boycott occurs when competitors agree to collectively refuse to deal with a particular firm or individual, which is a per se antitrust violation under the Sherman Act.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1

question: Competing brokers agreeing to divide a market by geographic territory or price range so that each firm has an exclusive set of customers is known as what illegal antitrust practice?
choice_a: Group boycotting
choice_b: Redlining
choice_c: Market allocation
choice_d: Steering
explanation: Market allocation agreements divide territories or customer bases among competitors to avoid competing with one another, and are treated as a per se violation of antitrust law.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1

question: Requiring a buyer to use a particular title company or mortgage lender as a condition of purchasing a home is an example of what antitrust violation?
choice_a: Market allocation
choice_b: Group boycotting
choice_c: Blockbusting
choice_d: A tie-in (tying) arrangement
explanation: A tying arrangement conditions the sale of one product or service (the home) on the purchase of another (a particular title or lending service), which can violate antitrust law and, in referral-fee contexts, RESPA as well.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1

question: Criminal violations of the Sherman Antitrust Act, such as price fixing among competing brokerages, can result in what type of penalties for individuals?
choice_a: Fines and/or imprisonment, since such violations may be prosecuted as felonies
choice_b: License suspension only, with no other penalty
choice_c: A written warning from the state licensing board
choice_d: Mandatory continuing education, with no financial penalty
explanation: The Sherman Act treats per se antitrust violations like price fixing as felonies, exposing individuals to substantial fines and potential imprisonment, in addition to civil liability.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1

question: Before making unsolicited telemarketing calls to consumers about real estate services, a licensee must check the phone numbers against what?
choice_a: The state bar association's referral list
choice_b: The National Do Not Call Registry
choice_c: The Multiple Listing Service directory
choice_d: The county property tax roll
explanation: The Telemarketing Sales Rule and Telephone Consumer Protection Act require telemarketers, including real estate licensees, to scrub call lists against the National Do Not Call Registry before calling consumers.
source_note: Telephone Consumer Protection Act, 47 U.S.C. § 227; Telemarketing Sales Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 310

question: Under Do-Not-Call rules, a licensee may generally still call a consumer whose number is on the National Do Not Call Registry if what exception applies?
choice_a: The consumer's number appeared in a phone book
choice_b: The call is made after 9:00 p.m.
choice_c: An established business relationship exists between the licensee and the consumer
choice_d: The licensee has fewer than five employees
explanation: The established business relationship exception allows calls to consumers with whom the caller has a recent transaction or inquiry-based relationship, subject to time limits set by the Telemarketing Sales Rule.

question: In addition to checking the National Do Not Call Registry, licensees who engage in telemarketing must also maintain what?
choice_a: A public list of all clients' phone numbers
choice_b: A recording of every call made, retained permanently
choice_c: A separate license specifically for telemarketing activity
choice_d: An internal, company-specific do-not-call list honoring any consumer's request not to be called again, regardless of registry status
explanation: Telemarketers must honor individual do-not-call requests by maintaining their own internal do-not-call list, independent of the National Registry, and must not call a number on that internal list again.

question: How often must telemarketers, including real estate licensees who cold-call prospects, check their call lists against the National Do Not Call Registry?
choice_a: At least once every 31 days
choice_b: Once per calendar year
choice_c: Only when a new employee is hired
choice_d: There is no required interval
explanation: The Telemarketing Sales Rule requires sellers and telemarketers to access the National Do Not Call Registry at least once every 31 days and remove matching numbers from their call lists.

question: Under the CAN-SPAM Act, commercial email advertisements sent by real estate licensees must include what?
choice_a: A notarized signature from the sender
choice_b: A clear and conspicuous opt-out mechanism, the sender's valid physical postal address, and accurate, non-deceptive header and subject line information
choice_c: A requirement that recipients pay a small fee to unsubscribe
choice_d: No sender-identifying information, to protect the licensee's privacy
explanation: The CAN-SPAM Act sets requirements for commercial email, including truthful header information, a functioning opt-out method, and disclosure of the sender's physical address.
source_note: CAN-SPAM Act of 2003, 15 U.S.C. § 7701 et seq.

question: When a licensee markets listings through social media or other internet platforms, which requirement continues to apply just as it would for print or broadcast advertising?
choice_a: No license-law advertising rules apply because social media is an informal, personal medium
choice_b: Only the platform's own terms of service govern the content, with no other legal requirements
choice_c: The advertisement must remain truthful, non-discriminatory under fair housing law, and identify the licensee or brokerage as required by license law
choice_d: Fair housing advertising rules apply only to newspaper and print advertisements
explanation: Fair housing advertising rules and license-law disclosure requirements apply regardless of the medium; social media and internet posts are treated as advertising and must be truthful, non-discriminatory, and properly identify the licensee.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); general license-law advertising disclosure requirements

question: A real estate licensee acting as a client's fiduciary owes a duty of confidentiality that generally prohibits disclosing what, absent the client's consent?
choice_a: Known material physical defects in the property that must be disclosed to all parties
choice_b: The property's public tax assessment record
choice_c: The property's legal description
choice_d: The client's motivation for buying or selling, and their willingness to accept a lower price or pay a higher price than initially stated
explanation: Fiduciary confidentiality protects a client's negotiating position and personal motivations, but it does not excuse a licensee from separately required disclosures of known material property defects to other parties.
source_note: Common law fiduciary duties of loyalty and confidentiality owed by an agent to a principal

question: A licensee's fiduciary duty of confidentiality to a former client generally continues for how long, absent a specific statutory duration or a waiver by the client?
choice_a: Indefinitely, even after the transaction closes or the agency relationship ends
choice_b: It ends automatically the day the transaction closes
choice_c: It ends when the client stops paying for representation
choice_d: It never applies once a licensee is representing a new client
explanation: Under general agency law, the duty of confidentiality is one of the few fiduciary duties that survives termination of the agency relationship and continues indefinitely unless the client consents to disclosure or a law requires it.
source_note: General agency law principles governing fiduciary duties

question: A licensee who deposits a client's earnest money into the brokerage's personal or general operating account rather than a separate trust/escrow account has committed what violation?
choice_a: Conversion of funds
choice_b: Commingling of funds
choice_c: Redlining
choice_d: Blockbusting
explanation: Commingling occurs when client trust funds are mixed with a broker's personal or operating funds instead of being held in a separate trust or escrow account, a violation of nearly all real estate license laws.
source_note: General real estate license law trust account requirements

question: When a broker uses client trust funds for a purpose other than that for which they were entrusted, such as paying the brokerage's business expenses, this more serious violation is called what?
choice_a: Commingling
choice_b: Steering
choice_c: Conversion
choice_d: Puffing
explanation: Conversion involves the actual unauthorized use of client trust funds for a purpose other than that for which they were entrusted, which is generally treated as a more serious violation than mere commingling.
source_note: General real estate license law trust account requirements

question: Why do real estate license laws require brokers to maintain a separate trust (escrow) account for client funds?
choice_a: To allow the broker to earn maximum interest on client deposits for the broker's own benefit
choice_b: To avoid any recordkeeping or reconciliation obligations
choice_c: Because federal law prohibits brokers from ever holding client funds
choice_d: To keep client funds segregated from the broker's own operating funds and protect them from being used for the broker's business expenses or personal use
explanation: Trust accounts exist to protect client funds by keeping them clearly separated from the broker's own money, reducing the risk of loss, commingling, or conversion.
source_note: General real estate license law trust account requirements

question: A licensee's duty of reasonable care and diligence with respect to property facts generally requires the licensee to do what?
choice_a: Conduct a reasonably diligent visual inspection and disclose known material facts, without acting as a guarantor of conditions beyond the licensee's expertise
choice_b: Personally certify the structural soundness of the property as an engineer would
choice_c: Guarantee that the property is free of all latent defects
choice_d: Rely solely on the seller's verbal assurances without independent inquiry
explanation: Licensees are expected to exercise reasonable care in observing and disclosing readily observable, material facts, but they are not held to the standard of a specialized inspector or engineer.
source_note: General agency and license-law duty-of-care principles

question: When a due diligence issue arises that falls outside a licensee's expertise, such as a suspected structural problem, a title defect, or a tax consequence of a transaction, what is the licensee's proper responsibility?
choice_a: Provide the client with the licensee's own best guess and move forward with the transaction
choice_b: Recommend that the client consult an appropriately licensed professional, such as a home inspector, attorney, or CPA, rather than render such advice personally
choice_c: Ignore the issue since it is outside the scope of the transaction
choice_d: Resolve the issue directly by drafting legal documents to address it
explanation: Licensees must recognize the limits of their expertise and refer clients to qualified professionals for legal, tax, structural, or other specialized matters, avoiding the unauthorized practice of another profession.
source_note: General license law prohibitions on unauthorized practice of law and other professions

question: A managing broker's supervisory responsibility over affiliated licensees generally includes which of the following?
choice_a: Only collecting commission splits, with no oversight of licensee conduct
choice_b: Supervision limited strictly to advertising content and nothing else
choice_c: Reviewing transaction documents, providing training, and ensuring licensees comply with license law, fiduciary duties, and fair housing and antitrust requirements
choice_d: No responsibility once a licensee has completed initial training
explanation: A supervising broker is generally responsible for actively overseeing affiliated licensees' compliance with license law and legal duties throughout the course of their affiliation, not just at the outset.
source_note: General broker supervisory duty under real estate license law

question: A supervising broker may permit an unlicensed assistant to perform which of the following tasks?
choice_a: Negotiating the price or terms of a purchase agreement on the broker's behalf
choice_b: Holding open houses and answering substantive questions about property condition or price
choice_c: Presenting offers and counteroffers directly to buyers and sellers
choice_d: Clerical and administrative tasks, such as scheduling appointment logistics, preparing marketing flyers, and answering phones
explanation: Unlicensed assistants may perform ministerial, clerical, and administrative functions, but activities requiring a real estate license, such as negotiating, presenting offers, or advising on price, are reserved for licensed individuals under the broker's supervision.
source_note: General license law restrictions on unlicensed assistant activities

question: Under the common law doctrine of respondeat superior, a broker may be held vicariously liable for what?
choice_a: The wrongful acts of licensees or employees committed within the scope of their employment or agency with the brokerage
choice_b: Only acts the broker personally witnessed
choice_c: Acts committed by a licensee entirely outside the scope of their real estate activities, such as a personal car accident unrelated to work
choice_d: Nothing, since brokers cannot be held liable for a licensee's conduct under any circumstance
explanation: Respondeat superior holds an employer or principal liable for the wrongful acts of an employee or agent performed within the scope of employment or agency, which underlies much of a broker's supervisory exposure.
source_note: Common law doctrine of respondeat superior

question: To help preserve a licensee's classification as an independent contractor rather than an employee, a broker's written independent contractor agreement should generally avoid controlling what, while still requiring compliance with license law and brokerage policy?
choice_a: Whether the licensee maintains an active real estate license
choice_b: The specific hours the licensee works and the day-to-day methods the licensee uses to generate business
choice_c: Whether the licensee complies with fair housing and antitrust law
choice_d: Whether commissions are paid according to the brokerage's compensation plan
explanation: Excessive control over the manner and means of a licensee's work, such as dictating specific hours or day-to-day sales methods, undermines independent contractor status under both the IRS common law test and IRC Section 3508.
source_note: 26 U.S.C. § 3508; IRS common law control test

question: When a broker permits a group of licensees to operate as a "team" within the brokerage, what ultimate responsibility does the broker retain?
choice_a: No responsibility, since team leaders fully assume all supervisory duties
choice_b: Responsibility only for the team's marketing materials, and nothing else
choice_c: Overall supervisory and regulatory responsibility for the team's compliance with license law and fiduciary duties, regardless of the team's internal branding or leadership structure
choice_d: Responsibility that automatically transfers to the team leader once the team is formed
explanation: Regardless of how a team brands or organizes itself internally, the supervising broker remains ultimately responsible under license law for the compliance and conduct of every licensee affiliated with the brokerage, including team members.
source_note: General broker supervisory duty under real estate license law
